Your posting asks for
Where I have done it
A decision cadence that shows next quarter’s revenue, and the levers to influence it in real time
The executive review with the CEO and COO on one drivers-and-levers model, traffic to revenue (BWZ). Forecast held within ±10% and re-cut as lines moved; when two shocks hit, a tornado across the levers showed what was still worth pulling.
Translate objectives into revenue targets, capacity models and headcount plans
A bottoms-up capacity model from call volume, connect rate and call length, used to set quota. It showed the ask for more advisors was wrong: the two we had had hours to spare. We did not hire, and revenue went from ~$30K to ~$130K a month in four to six months.
Prioritize leverage across acquisition, conversion, expansion and NRR
Every funnel step mapped across 16 publications; the constraint was lead handling, not traffic. Buyer base up ~30%. On retention: an automated post-sales program across a 14-country territory took churn from 30% to 8% (PressReader).
Align pricing and packaging with LTV, with Product and Finance
Pricing tested three ways at Omnie (fixed, per-response, banded monthly by usage) and settled on the one both sides could forecast; partner terms and margin-based compensation at BWZ.
Architect and maintain automation for outbound motions
An outbound engine at Omnie: 3,500 prospects in month one, 2,500+ a month after, ~5% replies, a 5:1 coverage rule. A project-triggered engine for the industrial firm that the reps correct from inside the CRM.
Own the forecast with Finance, closing the gap in CX forecasting
New-revenue forecasting within ±10%. I have run retention but not built a CX or renewal forecast as such; I would want to see where yours breaks before saying how I would close it.

Where I have done it
Be the accountability layer: tell leaders what activity it takes to hit the target
The capacity model told the advisors what attempts it took; weekly metrics and coaching held every tier 1–3 lead to an attempt. At Omnie, the 5:1 coverage rule told us how many lists we needed each month.
Stand your ground in executive forums; defend data integrity
Separated two shocks in one analysis and told the executive team to monetize the leads we had rather than buy more content. I was overruled, and the data was right. At Chef Joey, the revenue split I pulled from Stripe changed what the owner built the business around.
Own the quarterly review deck; standardize definitions and SLAs; lead qualification, attribution, pipeline hygiene
The L10 dashboard and review the executive team ran on; a lead-tiering model with a response standard (first response ~12 hours to 30 minutes); one written definition and one source per metric; one record per account.
Ultimate responsibility for the CRM; architectural direction; an AI-enhanced stack for hygiene and routing
Salesforce re-architected around how the business sells, now capturing ~95% of new opportunities; dedup and hygiene automation; Chili Piper routing; AI call grading (~30% to 75–80%); outreach drafted by AI and approved by a rep. HubSpot, Zoho and Dynamics as well.
Manage and mentor the RevOps Analyst; build the function. Not a first-time manager
A team of four across 14 countries (two contract reps, a reseller organization, a BDR); a BDR hired, trained and managed; advisors coached; decision logs and training curricula so a client’s own team could run what I built.
The parts I have not done: run RevOps where ARR, NRR and LTV/CAC were the scoreboard (my programs were lead-gen and services revenue), built a CX forecast, or reported to a board rather than a CEO and COO; and I have gone deeper in Salesforce than HubSpot. I would rather say that here, and I am confident these are bridgeable.
How I think
Revenue broken into its pieces, the drivers under each, and the levers a team can actually pull.
Every business I have worked with, I have ended up drawing something like this. Every lever on it has a metric, a source of truth, an owner, a review cadence, and a guard against gaming it.
A project gets attention when it moves a line that rolls up to the number. That takes most of the subjectivity out of quarterly priorities.
The CEO and the sales leader own the number. The model, the source of truth, the forecast and the cadence are the part I own.

How I think · three lever cards, opened
Every lever reads the same way: one metric, the funnel under it, the guards beside it. Three I have pulled.
SDR / BDR capacity
At Black & White Zebra the ask was more advisors. A capacity model built from call volume, connect rate and call length said the two we had were working leads by preference, with hours to spare. It set quota, and we did not hire.
Website conversion
After the two shocks it had the most headroom left, so the last six months went there: every two weeks, a hypothesis for one funnel step, scoped, built and run hands-off. Step 1 to 2 up about 45%, submissions per click up 25%.
Target account quality
At Omnie, two ICP hypotheses run in parallel for two months; the data picked one, and the profile narrowed each round after. At the industrial firm, the win history recomputed by segment put retrofit on the table for the first time.

Forecast and cadence on the Revenue node
Situation
16 software-buyer publications, about $30K a month from lead generation, and every funnel step measured somewhere but not in one place. Nobody could say which step cost the most.
The decision
Map every step, then fix what it showed before asking for anything new. It was not a traffic problem: leads were worked by preference, not by tier. So instead of hiring: territory routing, direct booking, a tiering model, a capacity model for quota, weekly metrics and coaching, and the case for margin-based commission.
Two shocks, and the argument I lost
About eight months in, generative search cut into leads and the prompt feeding 70% of them was switched off, rightly, for the company. I separated the two shocks in one analysis, ran a tornado across what was left, and put the conclusion to the executive team plainly: monetize the leads we had, not more content. I was overruled; a quarter of content ranked and barely converted. The last six months went to the bi-weekly experiment program.

In your posting’s terms: pricing and packaging tested against what the business could forecast; outbound automation architected and maintained; a defined handoff from closed-won into onboarding. What I would do differently: take the path of least resistance first; two sellers chasing two markets is one seller in each.

Situation
A bootstrapped company that plugged a whole customer-service function, people and help-desk stack, into online stores. On day one: a founder who had never sold, two account executives, an empty CRM and a PowerPoint. No ICP, no sales journey, almost no capital.
The decision
Build reach first, because two people cannot find a market by hand. Then test the ICP rather than argue about it: two hypotheses run in parallel for two months, and the data said the founder was right. Then write the journey down, discovery to close to onboarding, so the system carried the number and an agency and a BDR could be put onto it.
How it ran
A new list every two to four weeks, targeting adjusted from the last one; a five-to-one coverage rule set how many lists we needed. Pricing tested three ways and settled on banded monthly fees, because the number had to be forecastable on both sides.

Situation
A Calgary cooking-experience company with three revenue lines, selling the easiest one, public classes. About two inquiries a week, no CRM, five tools that did not talk to each other, and no way to say which line the money came from.
The decision
There was nothing to follow, so I pulled every transaction out of Stripe and split it by line. Corporate was about half the revenue, far better per hour, and the part the owner enjoyed most. The question changed from “how do we get more traffic” to “do you want to build this business around corporate.” He said yes.
What I built
In about four weeks: a site rebuilt around the corporate buyer, a CRM with one pipeline per line, automation that makes the system disappear, outbound to business accounts, and one trusted source per metric. Measurement came before any spend. No retainer; the two owners run it themselves.
2 → 14
Inbound leads a week, most of the new ones corporate. No paid traffic.
~$2K → ~$20K
Pipeline created per week, from the client’s CRM, May to October 2026
5 → 1
Tools: five disconnected to one system of record
In your posting’s terms: data turned into the decision that mattered; one standard definition and one source per metric; technology that serves the strategy, and one thing I should not have built. What I would do differently: set a decision date on day one, and not over-build for the line we had just de-emphasized.
In your posting’s terms: architectural direction for a CRM nobody used; AI-assisted hygiene, routing and scoring with people on every conversation; a process problem that looked like a systems one; documentation so the client’s own analyst could run it.

Situation
A turnkey engineering and construction firm selling into large energy and industrial projects. Six reps, about twenty resellers, a Salesforce org nobody used, and no clean picture of where their own wins came from. The ask was more meetings; discovery said the problem sat upstream.
The decision
Map how revenue moves through the business first. That produced two segments across six industries and two motions, and surfaced the thing everything hangs on: nothing starts until a project is announced. So I rebuilt Salesforce around a project object, owned the data layer rather than renting it, and built the outreach engine to be tuned by the reps from inside the CRM.
Result so far
Structural, and I would rather say that plainly. The first sends are about to start, so there is no pipeline number yet. What changed is what the business can see: a formal revenue map for the first time, reporting that answers where wins come from, and a pre-approval gap that was invisible before and is now on the table.
~95%
Of new opportunities now land in Salesforce, from an org that held only closed-won and closed-lost
25,000+
Companies in an owned market layer, replacing $20–50K a year of paid data
How I would like to start
If you are considering me, I would be glad to do a small piece of the job as part of the process.
Alongside whatever your process normally involves, I would like to put together a short first-quarter plan for Athennian from one or two conversations about what is going well and what is getting in the way. You would have something concrete of mine to react to, rather than only my answers to questions. Your posting asks this role to translate business objectives into revenue targets, capacity models and headcount plans; this would be a first, rough pass at that from the outside, including where I think the CX forecast gap sits.
It is how I was hired at Black & White Zebra, and the plan I wrote then turned out to be roughly the one I ran. That is one example, not a guarantee.
What it would involve
  • One or two conversations; the questions I would ask in a first week
  • A written 30, 60, 90-day plan: the two or three things I would focus on first, what I would measure early, and what I would leave alone
  • Nothing needed from your systems or data; I would be clear about where I am guessing
  • A plan you can keep, whatever you decide
It is only an offer. If it does not fit how you hire, I am glad to go through the usual steps.
What I am looking for
Director of Revenue Operations at Athennian. I am in Calgary, so the office is easy. Full-time, and for the long term.
